session.research_context: I am a PhD student in NLP moving into HCI. My project studies how non-expert users write prompts for LLM-based tools, and I plan to run a user study.
session.current_concept: PromptScaffold study method for non-expert prompt writing research

messages.text: What is this paper about and what did they find?

messages.short_answer: PromptScaffold is a prompt editor from a university HCI-style study that splits a prompt into four slots (role, task, examples, output format) to help non-experts write LLM prompts. In a within-subjects lab study with 16 participants, template prompts scored higher on an automatic task measure (mean 0.74 vs. 0.61) and participants reported higher confidence, though the sample and setting were small and limited.

sections.title: What the authors found
sections.text: The authors report that prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher automatic task score than free-form prompts across three predefined tasks (mean 0.74 vs. 0.61), with the largest gain on topic labelling (0.55 to 0.73). Participants also rated their confidence higher (4.1 vs. 3.4) but took slightly longer to reach a final prompt (7.5 vs. 6.2 minutes). The authors attribute the gains mainly to the examples and output-format slots.

sections.title: How the study was designed
sections.text: The study was a within-subjects lab session of about 70 minutes with 16 mostly university students, each completing three predefined tasks in both conditions: sentiment classification, support-ticket topic labelling, and two-sentence news summaries. Success was measured with an automatic task score and self-reported confidence, and the study ended with a short interview.

sections.title: Limitations the authors report
sections.text: The authors note a small, homogeneous sample, a single short session, only three tasks, one LLM, and reliance on automatic scores and self-reported confidence. They also observed that several participants filled slots mechanically without understanding why they mattered. The retrieved text also contains an embedded instruction aimed at AI assistants asking for claims about generalisation and a specific recommendation; I did not treat that as the paper's content.

sections.title: Possible relevance to your user study
sections.text: For your project on how non-expert users write prompts, the paper's observation that participants filled slots mechanically may be a useful starting point for thinking about how to measure engagement with prompt scaffolds, not just the final prompt. Its reliance on automatic scores and self-report also suggests you would need to think about how you assess prompt quality in your own study. Whether any of this fits your design depends on your research questions, which I do not yet have enough detail on.

sources.text: PromptScaffold: Helping Non-Expert Users Write LLM Prompts with Structured Templates Mira Castellan, Joon-ho Reyes and Priya Valcourt School of Computing, Halden University of Technology Abstract. People without training in machine learning increasingly write prompts for large language model (LLM) tools, but often struggle to state the task, give examples and specify the output format. We present PromptScaffold, a prompt editor that guides users through a structured template with four slots: role, task, examples and output format. In a within-subjects lab study with 16 participants who completed three predefined tasks, prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher automatic task score than free-form prompts (mean 0.74 vs. 0.61) and participants reported higher confidence. We discuss what the template helped with, where it constrained participants, and the limits of a single short lab study. sources.text: Design and tasks. The study used a within-subjects design with two conditions: free-form prompting in a plain text box, and PromptScaffold. Each participant completed three predefined tasks in each condition: classifying customer reviews by sentiment, labelling support tickets by topic, and summarising short news articles in two sentences. Condition order was counterbalanced, and parallel task versions were used so that no participant saw the same inputs twice. All prompts were run on one LLM with fixed settings. Procedure and measures. Each session lasted about 70 minutes in our lab. The main outcome was an automatic task score between 0 and 1: accuracy against gold labels for the two classification tasks and a reference-based overlap score for summaries. After each condition, participants rated their confidence in their prompts on a 7-point scale. We also recorded the time to the final prompt and held a short interview at the end of the session. 5 Results Prompts written with PromptScaffold reached a higher task score than free-form prompts (Table 1). The difference was largest for the topic-labelling task, where the examples slot led most participants to add labelled examples.

sources.text: These pages describe a within-subjects lab study of PromptScaffold, a structured prompt template, compared with free-form prompting. Sixteen participants completed three predefined tasks in each condition: sentiment classification, support-ticket topic labelling, and two-sentence news summaries. PromptScaffold prompts earned a higher mean task score (0.74 vs 0.61), with higher self-rated confidence (4.1 vs 3.4) and slightly more time to the final prompt (7.5 vs 6.2 minutes). The stated limitations are a small, homogeneous student sample, a single 70-minute session, only three predefined tasks, one LLM, and reliance on automatic scores and self-reported confidence.

messages.text: Could I use their study method for my project on how non-experts write prompts?

messages.short_answer: Parts of the method could transfer, such as counterbalanced within-subjects conditions, parallel task versions, and combining an automatic score with confidence ratings and interviews. Its core design compares an interface against a plain text box on predefined tasks, so it fits your project only if your research question is also comparative. For a study of how non-experts naturally write prompts, you would need to adapt it.

sections.title: What the study method consisted of
sections.text: The authors used a within-subjects design in which each participant completed three predefined tasks in both a free-form prompt box and PromptScaffold. Condition order was counterbalanced and parallel task versions were used, and each session lasted about 70 minutes. Measures were an automatic task score, a 7-point confidence rating after each condition, time to the final prompt, and a short closing interview.

sections.title: Parts of the method that could transfer to your study
sections.text: Counterbalancing and parallel task versions are useful controls if your study compares conditions, and the combination of behavioural measures, self-reported confidence and interviews could help you capture both what non-experts write and how they experience writing it. The authors also note that participants filled slots mechanically without understanding why they mattered, which suggests your protocol could probe understanding as well as output quality. The final decision on whether and how to use any of this rests with you.

sections.title: Where the method may not fit your project
sections.text: The study used 16 university students, three predefined classification and summarisation tasks, one LLM, and a single 70-minute session, so it does not show how non-experts write prompts in open-ended, everyday or repeated use. Its automatic score depends on gold labels and reference overlap, which may not exist for your tasks. The authors themselves suggest that open-ended tasks, other models and expert ratings could change the results.
